31UMkg3CSzc.description:
Holding a cup of coffee still, arm bent, feels like the easiest thing you will do today. Inside your arm it is not.

Your elbow is a lever with the pivot at the joint. The cup sits in your hand, roughly 30 to 35 centimetres out. The muscles that bend your elbow attach only a few centimetres from the pivot - for the biceps, the peak lever arm measured in cadaver arms is 4.2 to 5.4 cm. To balance a load that far out from that close in, they have to pull about seven times its weight. The biceps does not do it alone: brachialis and brachioradialis share the work, and how they split it changes with the position of your hand.

That short lever is not a design flaw. The same ratio works the other way for movement: a small shortening near the joint swings your hand through a much larger arc, several times faster. Your arm traded force for speed.

Sources:
https://nmbl.stanford.edu/publications/pdf/Murray2002.pdf
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526813/
31UMkg3CSzc.title: Every Sip Costs Your Muscles Seven Cups

AeBnm-AbY6E.description:
Something went through your head while you read that. It was made about fifteen kilometres up, when a cosmic ray from somewhere in the galaxy hit an air molecule and burst into a shower of debris.

What reaches the ground is one splinter of that shower: a muon. About one of them crosses a hand-sized patch of you every second, and it goes through skin, skull and bone without being slowed enough to notice.

Here is the part nobody uses. A muon lives about 2.2 microseconds. Even at nearly light speed that buys it only a few hundred metres, and the fall from fifteen kilometres takes roughly fifty microseconds - more than twenty of its lifetimes. The naive sum says it should be long gone before it gets anywhere near you.

It arrives anyway, because at that speed its clock runs slow. That is special relativity, and it is not something demonstrated once in a lab with an accelerator. It is being demonstrated through your skull about once a second, and has been every second you have been alive.

You are not watching a relativity experiment. You are standing in one.

Sources:
https://pdg.lbl.gov/2022/reviews/rpp2022-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf
https://pdg.lbl.gov/2023/listings/rpp2023-list-muon.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muon
https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Particles/muonatm.html
AeBnm-AbY6E.title: Your Body Is A Cosmic Ray Detector

You are not solid. Every atom in your body is mostly empty space — and what
holds it together isn't matter, it's a field you can't see.

But here's the part almost nobody gets right: the Higgs field only explains
about 1% of your body weight. The other 99% is pure binding energy — light
and motion, trapped inside your protons and held in place.

D82fo98Gbdw.description:
Hold a magnet against your arm and nothing happens. That is not because your body is neutral. It is because the push is very, very small.

Water is diamagnetic. Put it in a magnetic field and it develops a faint field of its own pointing the wrong way, so the field pushes it out instead of pulling it in. You are mostly water. Which means every magnetic field you have ever walked through has pushed you away - by an amount far too small to feel, and never once equal to zero.

And no, it is not the iron in your blood. That iron sits bound inside a haemoglobin molecule, not as loose metal, and it does not answer a magnet the way a nail does. The myth is the boring version of this. The truth is that all of you responds, faintly, all the time.

The push scales with the field, and fields can be made enormous. In 1997 a solenoid in Nijmegen running at about 16 tesla held a live frog in mid-air - a very young one, an object of roughly ten millimetres radius, not the fist-sized animal people picture. Grasshoppers, water drops, flowers and hazelnuts went up in the same bore. Thirteen years later a magnet with a room-temperature bore did the same to a laboratory mouse.

A frog, then a mouse. Nobody has built the magnet for a person, and this is a consequence being worked out rather than an experiment anyone has run - but nothing in the physics says the sequence stops.

Sources:
https://materias.df.uba.ar/ft1a2015c2/files/2015/09/Frog_levitation_Eur_J_Phys_Geim.pdf
https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20100033545
D82fo98Gbdw.title: Your Body Is Diamagnetic

FTGhQcpG_RA.description:
You press a finger against glass and feel a surface. There is no surface.

Atoms have no edge. An electron cloud is a probability distribution, not a shell, so there is nothing there for two surfaces to meet along. What actually stops your finger is the Pauli exclusion principle: as the electron clouds of your skin and the glass overlap, the electrons are forced into higher energy states, and the energy climbs so steeply that the push feels like a wall instead of a spring. The push is electromagnetic. How absolutely it refuses to let you through is Pauli.

And no, there is no gap. The clouds do overlap and interact — that overlap is the push. Nothing you feel is fake: the fingerprint, the grip, the pain when you hit a wall are all exactly what a force field feels like when it is stiff enough. "Solid" was the only illusion in the room.

Without the Pauli exclusion principle, matter would not hold its shape at all. Dyson and Lenard proved that in 1967.

Hx_Ob-85IL4.description:
Stand up straight. There is a point about halfway up you that every equation of motion treats as your entire body - and it is not a place. It is an average, recomputed from wherever your limbs happen to be.

Raise your arms and it climbs. Lean and it slides. Bend far enough forward and it travels out through the front of you and hangs in open air, in a spot where there is no body at all. Standing normally it is inside you: a little above the middle, about 57% of your height in men and 55% in women, measured from the floor to the top of your head, and roughly an inch in front of the top of the second sacral vertebra. It shifts with build and posture.

Then the part that is not bookkeeping. The instant your feet leave the floor, that point is locked onto a curve and nothing you do can move it. Not your arms, not your legs, not a twist. Moving one part of you toward something moves the rest of you away by exactly as much, so only gravity gets a say. Your jump is decided before you are airborne, and everything after that is decoration.

Which is why a high jumper can arch backwards over the bar while that point passes underneath it. The body clears. The point never has to.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_mass
https://www.physics.unlv.edu/~jeffery/astro/mechanics/center_of_mass_fosbury_flop.html
https://chiro.org/ACAPress/Body_Alignment.html
Hx_Ob-85IL4.title: Your Center Of Gravity Leaves Your Body

J2uuDDU1j1Y.description:
Push down into your chair. That heaviness is real, but it is not gravity. It is the seat pushing up into you.

Gravity pulls on every atom of your body at once, evenly, all the way through. A nerve works by being deformed — something has to press one part of you against another part of you. A pull that acts on every part equally leaves nothing for a nerve to compare, so no nerve you own can sample it. What you actually feel is the contact force: the chair against your back and your thighs, the floor against your soles, your shoes against your feet.

A bathroom scale works the same way. It never measures gravity. It measures how hard it is pushing back at you. That is why a lift accelerating upward makes the number climb exactly as though gravity had strengthened — and why an accelerometer in free fall reads zero while the field around it is still fully present. The measurable quantity is proper acceleration, not gravity. Your inner ear is an accelerometer. It has been reading the chair this whole time.

Take the support away and the pull is unchanged at full strength, but the sensation vanishes completely. That is what the half-second of a jump actually is. It is the only time in your life you have ever been alone with gravity, and it feels like nothing at all.

Einstein got there in 1907 and called it the happiest thought of his life: for an observer falling freely, the gravitational field does not exist. Not weakened — locally unmeasurable.

Which is what the space station really is. At that altitude Earth's gravity is still about 90 percent of what it is at the surface. NASA states that directly, and NASA also says outright that calling it "zero gravity" is misleading. The crew are not floating because the pull has gone. They are falling around the Earth, and the station and everything in it are falling with them, so nothing is pushing on anybody. They are living permanently in the state you occupy for half a second at the top of a jump.

One caveat the 50 seconds had no room for, and it is the honest one. Gravity is not undetectable full stop — it is undetectable *locally*. Across an extended body the field is very slightly non-uniform, and that tidal gradient is real and measurable. Quantified for a person standing on Earth, across a 1.8 m body it comes to roughly 5.5 x 10^-6 m/s2 — about 0.6 millionths of g, around one part in 1.8 million of your body weight. Hundreds of thousands of times below any sensory threshold you own. So the claim is not "gravity cannot be measured." The claim is that nothing in your body can sample it. That one holds.

The pull never changed. Only the pushing did.

O9uV2CMhYOo.description:
The bone in your thigh is not an inert beam. Load it - stand, step, jump - and a small voltage appears across it.

Two things produce that voltage. The collagen fibres that form bone's organic scaffold are piezoelectric: shear them and charge shifts across them. Yasuda reported it in dry bone in 1954, and Fukada and Yasuda confirmed it in 1957. In wet, living bone, though, the larger share comes from something else - fluid pushed through the bone's microscopic canals past charged walls, a streaming potential.

The collagen half is the same physics that makes the spark in a push-button lighter. The lighter uses a ceramic. Your skeleton uses a protein it built itself.

Whether these voltages help decide how bone rebuilds itself under load is still a hypothesis, not a settled fact.

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/bioengineering-and-biotechnology/articles/10.3389/fbioe.2021.705199/full
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9243952/
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5828134/
Original paper: E. Fukada and I. Yasuda, J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 12, 1158 (1957)
O9uV2CMhYOo.title: Bone Is Piezoelectric, Like A Gas Lighter

QCDhWMbHVZw.description:
You cannot stand still. Not on a scale, not in bed, not for one beat of your heart.

Each heartbeat sends about 70 millilitres of blood up out of your heart and around the arch of your aorta, the main artery. The pressure differences that push that blood along also push back on the rest of you, so your whole body is rocked to and fro with every beat - a small movement one way, then a larger one the other way. The effect has a name, the ballistocardiogram, and it is large enough for a scale to show. In 1877, J. W. Gordon described watching the index of a weighing scale move in time with the pulse of a man standing on it. Today a force sensor under a bed can count heartbeats without touching the sleeper.

Sources, in the order the video makes the claims:
The whole body is rocked by each beat, and the force travels through pressure gradients in the ascending and descending aorta (Kim et al., Scientific Reports, 2016): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4977514/
The rocking has a fixed pattern - an early, smaller footward deflection (I wave), then the largest one headward (J wave) (Sadek, BCG review, 2018): https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.00951
Resting stroke volume, 60 to 100 mL in healthy adults - "about seventy" sits inside it (StatPearls): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547686/
The scale that moved with the pulse - Gordon, J. W. (1877), "Certain molar movements of the human body produced by the circulation of the blood", Journal of Anatomy and Physiology 11, 533-536: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1309740/
A load cell under a bed detecting heartbeats with no skin contact, plus a summary of Gordon's observation (Albukhari et al., Sensors, 2019): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6470700/
Pulse read from the tiny movement of the head on ordinary video - the same reaction, seen by a camera (Balakrishnan, Durand & Guttag, CVPR 2013): https://people.csail.mit.edu/mrub/vidmag/papers/Balakrishnan_Detecting_Pulse_from_2013_CVPR_paper.pdf
QCDhWMbHVZw.title: Nobody Stands Still For A Single Heartbeat

TEipugAb-GE.description:
Cover one nostril and breathe. Now swap sides. One of them is moving most of your air, and the other has been narrowed — not by a cold, not by a deviated septum, and not by accident.

This is the nasal cycle. Erectile tissue on your turbinates and the front of your septum fills with blood and swells inward on one side while the other side opens. It has been measured since Kayser described it in 1895, and it runs in roughly 70-80 % of healthy adults: Hasegawa and Kern put 50 people on continuous rhinomanometry at 15-minute intervals for about seven hours and found a clearly defined cycle in 72 % of them. Most people, not everyone. If you check and both sides feel equal, the acyclic pattern is documented and normal — that is your nose, not an error in the video.

There is no single switching time, and anyone who gives you one is guessing. Kahana-Zweig and colleagues measured 33 healthy people continuously for 24 hours: every subject changed dominant nostril at least once, mean dominance about 2 hours awake and 4.5 hours asleep, with individual phases running from 15 minutes to over 10 hours. A fortyfold spread. Lying on one side congests the down-side nostril, so your own position moves it too.

The part that makes it worth 50 seconds: the narrowed side is not resting, it is working a different shift. The open passage carries about two thirds of the airflow and pays for it — a computational model of the airway predicts severe drying of the airway surface liquid along 48 % of the anterior region of the open side, which stalls the mucus conveyor that carries trapped dust and microbes out of your nose. The congested side, spared that load, stays wet enough to keep that cleaning system running. Then they trade. Your total airflow barely changes, which is exactly why you have never noticed. Two passages alternating between breathing and cleaning, swapping before either one dries out. That is the best explanation we have and it comes from modelling, not from a direct measurement inside a living nose — worth saying plainly.

One thing this video deliberately does not claim: that the open nostril tells you which brain hemisphere is active, or that one side calms you and the other energises you. That is the most repeated claim attached to this topic and it is not settled — studies disagree even on the direction of the effect, and Thaploo et al. (2024) found nasal-cycle lateralisation not reflected in olfactory bulb volumes or cerebral activations. The mechanism above is interesting enough without it.

cbUPlcHJSFs.description:
Hold your palm up right now. Touch your thumb to your smallest finger, bend your wrist forward, and count the cords that stand up. Most people see two. Some see one.

The thin one in the middle is the tendon of the palmaris longus, a muscle running the whole length of your forearm — and a substantial minority of people are simply built without it.

How many is where this gets interesting. Worldwide the pooled figure is about one in five: 20.25 % across 26 studies (Yammine, Clinical Anatomy, 2013), which the meta-analysis itself notes is higher than the 14-15 % that gets copied around. But that pooled number hides one of the widest population ranges in human anatomy — roughly 2.71 % in East and Southeast African populations, 4.5 % East Asian, 11.3 % African, 26.16 % South and Southeast Asian, 26.3 % Caucasian, 34.13 % Turkish, 41.7 % Arab Middle Eastern. A fifteenfold spread. So "one in five" is a real global average and a bad prediction about you personally, and if your own count disagrees with the video, that is the data, not an error.

The payoff: missing it costs you nothing anyone has been able to measure. When researchers tested 418 people aged 7 to 85, they found no statistically significant difference in grip or pinch strength between those who had the tendon and those who did not (Sebastin et al., J Hand Surg Br, 2005). That is one study on one cohort, so take it as measured rather than settled — but it is exactly why hand surgeons reach for this tendon first when they need a graft. Long, flat, easy to harvest, and losing it does not show up in your hand. The cord that pulls almost nothing is the one that gets woven into somebody's rebuilt ligament.

Two things this video does not claim. It does not say the muscle does nothing — it contributes minimally to wrist flexion, and minimally is not nothing. And it does not say evolution is deleting it: there is no evidence of a directional trend in living populations. It is an old, stable variation, not a disappearance in progress.

fI5VJxcCe84.description:
Drag a feather along your own arm and nothing happens. Hand it to somebody else, let them trace the exact same path, and you flinch.

Before your arm even moves, your brain sends a copy of that motor command ahead to the cerebellum, which predicts the touch the movement is about to produce. Whatever the prediction covers gets subtracted before it ever reaches you. That is why an identical touch is rated less intense and less tickly when you are the one producing it. Route the same movement through a robot and add a delay of 100 to 200 ms, and the tickle comes straight back.

Here is the part that is not trivia. In a 2003 Science study, six pairs of people took turns pressing each other's finger and were told to match the force exactly. In that experiment the force climbed by a mean of about 38 % on every turn, and nobody was cheating — each side honestly felt the other one hit harder, because your own force always lands quieter.

Two things this video deliberately does not claim. It does not claim nobody can tickle themselves — a delay restores it in anyone. And it does not claim science has explained tickling: the laughter kind (gargalesis) is still open. This is about light touch and sensory attenuation, which is the part that is actually settled.

grbzcXjIBSw.description:
The morning after the Challenger exploded in January 1986, psychologist Ulric
Neisser handed a questionnaire to 106 students: where were you when you heard?

Two and a half years later he found the same students and asked again — without
showing them what they'd written.

The mean accuracy score was 2.95 out of 7. Around a quarter recalled a completely
different source than the one they'd recorded the day after. And their confidence,
averaging 4.17 out of 5, predicted almost nothing about whether they were right.

Then he showed them their own handwriting from 1986. Some looked at the page,
recognised the writing as theirs — and kept the newer memory anyway.

Neisser and Harsch called them "phantom flashbulbs": memories that feel
photographic and are simply wrong.

SOURCES
Neisser, U. & Harsch, N. (1992). "Phantom flashbulbs: False recollections of
hearing the news about Challenger," in Affect and Accuracy in Recall, Cambridge
University Press.

jtcVdlnVrkc.description:
Your eyes jump about three times a second. During every one of those jumps
your brain shuts vision off — because the smear would be useless to you.

Add those gaps up and it comes to a rough estimate of forty minutes a day
spent blind. You never notice, because your brain fills the holes by
stretching the next image backwards in time.

Test it yourself: glance at a ticking clock. The first second looks longer.
That stretched second is the hole.

mkOl6-Zz3OM.description:
Say something out loud. That sound reached your inner ear by two routes at once, and only one of those routes exists outside your head.

The obvious route is the air: sound leaves your mouth, curves around the outside of your head and arrives at your ear canal. That is air conduction, and it is the only one most people know about. The second route runs through you. Speaking shakes your jaw and your skull, and bone carries that vibration inward directly to the inner ear.

How the two compare was measured directly. Reinfeldt, Ostli, Hakansson and Stenfelt put 20 normal-hearing adults aged 23 to 34 in a custom 1.2 kg ear-muff, built to attenuate air-conducted sound by at least 20 dB without inducing an occlusion effect, and compared the two contributions phoneme by phoneme. Their finding, in their own words: the air-conducted and bone-conducted components are approximately the same order of magnitude — and strongly frequency dependent. Between 1 and 2 kHz the bone component led for most of the ten phonemes tested: roughly 12 dB above the air component for the nasals /m/ and /n/, and about 15 dB above it at 2 kHz for the back vowel /o/. Von Bekesy reached the same order-of-magnitude conclusion back in 1949. Porschmann put the bone-dominant band at 0.7 to 1.2 kHz.

So which route is louder depends on the sound you are making. There is no single percentage, and anyone handing you one has quietly rounded off the frequency dependence.

Now the part that is actually about you. A microphone sits out in the air. It receives the air-conducted component and nothing else, because the bone-conducted component never enters the air at all. The same is true of every other person in the room. The blend of air and bone that you have listened to your entire life is assembled inside your own skull, has never reached another human being, and cannot be captured by any device that has ever been built. The discomfort of hearing the recording even has a name in the literature — voice confrontation, Holzman and Rousey, 1966.

Which inverts the usual framing. The recording is not the weird version of your voice. It is the public version. The private one is unrecordable, and it belongs to exactly one listener.

One thing this video deliberately does not say: that bone conduction "boosts the low frequencies, which is why you sound deeper to yourself". It is the single most repeated line on this topic and the primary measurements do not support it as stated — Reinfeldt found bone dominance in the 1 to 2 kHz mid-range, and Porschmann found the air component dominating below 0.7 kHz. If you want to explain why a recording sounds unfamiliar, the honest version is that the spectral balance is different because one of two pathways has been removed. Not that the bass was subtracted.

rvRDVWm8y4Q.description:
In 1815 Mount Tambora erupted in Indonesia — the most powerful eruption in
recorded history. The sulphur it threw into the stratosphere froze into a
veil of droplets that dimmed the sun across the whole planet.

The next year, 1816, went down as the Year Without a Summer. Snow fell in
June. Harvests failed across Europe and North America. Famine followed.

That same rain-soaked summer, a group of writers were stuck indoors beside
Lake Geneva and dared each other to write a ghost story. One of them was
eighteen years old. Her name was Mary Shelley, and what she started that
week became Frankenstein.

tWgJRVj4fIo.description:
Breathe out until nothing is left. You never get there. After the hardest exhale you can make, about 1 to 1.2 litres of air is still in your chest.

It is not weak muscles. As you push, the smallest airways - the ones with no cartilage holding them open - pinch shut before you finish, like the neck of a balloon, and seal the rest of the air behind them. That leftover air is your residual volume, and it is doing a job: it holds your air sacs open and keeps gas exchange going between one breath and the next.

Your lungs were not empty before you were born either. They were full of liquid, about a hundred times harder to move than air. Your first breaths drove that liquid deeper into the lungs, through the airway walls and into the surrounding tissue - over the first few breaths, not in one. The first of them was the hardest breath of your life. Since then the space inside your lungs has never once been empty. The air in it changes with every breath; the space never clears.

Hold up both hands. They are the same shape built twice, and they will never stack, because one is simply the mirror of the other.

That refusal goes all the way down. Molecules are handed too. A mirror twin has every atom in the same place and every bond the same length, and it still will not overlay on the original.

Your body picked one side and only ever builds on that side. Every protein you have ever made was assembled from left-handed pieces, and your ribosome will not accept the other one.

Which means half of all possible chemistry is food you can look at, smell, even taste, and never actually use. Mirror sugar still tastes sweet, because the sweet sensor on your tongue cannot tell the two apart. Your tongue is fooled. Your metabolism is not - your body gets almost nothing out of it.

A mirrored copy of you would sit down at a full table and slowly starve, because nothing on it would fit.

Now hold up both hands.
